content: Cefiderocol is indicated for the treatment of complicated urinary tract infections (cUTI), including pyelonephritis, caused by susceptible Gram-negative microorganisms. The recommended dosage is 2 grams administered intravenously every 8 hours for a duration of 7 to 14 days. The length of therapy should be determined based on the severity of the infection and the patient’s clinical status, with a maximum duration of 14 days. Cefiderocol is also indicated for the treatment of hospital-acquired bacterial pneumonia (HABP) and ventilator-associated bacterial pneumonia (VABP) caused by susceptible Gram-negative microorganisms. The recommended dosage is 2 grams intravenously every 8 hours for 7 to 14 days. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of antibacterial drugs, cefiderocol should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy selection. The safety and efficacy of cefiderocol have not been established in certain populations. Elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function, so dose selection should be cautious, and renal function should be monitored closely. Cefiderocol may decrease the effects of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. It is recommended to avoid or use an alternative drug. Oral microbiota products contain bacterial spores, and coadministration with antibacterial agents may reduce their efficacy. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Cefiderocol increases the toxicity of amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, plazomicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Caution should be exercised, and patients should be monitored closely. Cephalosporins, including cefiderocol, may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. Cefiderocol may decrease the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors such as atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, cosibelimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution is advised, and patients should be monitored closely, as coadministration may interfere with the therapeutic efficacy of these agents. Cefiderocol may increase the effects of warfarin through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is recommended. Severe hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis and serious skin reactions, have been reported with cefiderocol. These reactions are more likely in individuals with a history of beta-lactam hypersensitivity or sensitivity to multiple allergens. Therapy should be discontinued immediately if an allergic reaction occurs. Cephalosporins, including cefiderocol, may trigger seizures, particularly in patients with a history of epilepsy or when recommended dosages are exceeded due to renal impairment. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus, encephalopathy, coma, asterixis, neuromuscular excitability, and myoclonia have been reported. If central nervous system (CNS) adverse reactions, including seizures, occur, patients should undergo a neurological evaluation to determine whether treatment should be discontinued. Dosage adjustments are required for patients receiving continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT), including CVVH, CVVHD, and CVVHDF. Dosage should be based on the effluent flow rate. Changes in residual renal function during CRRT may necessitate dosage modifications. Prescribing cefiderocol in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection or a prophylactic indication is unlikely to provide benefit and may increase the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. There are no available data on the use of cefiderocol in pregnant women to evaluate the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Published data on cephalosporin use in pregnant women over several decades have not established drug-associated risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. It is unknown whether cefiderocol is excreted into human milk, but cefiderocol-derived radioactivity has been detected in the milk of lactating rats. When a drug is present in animal milk, it is likely to be present in human milk. No information is available on the effects of cefiderocol on the breastfed infant or milk production. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration prior to administration whenever the solution and container permit. Cefiderocol infusions are clear, colorless solutions. Any unused solution in the vial should be discarded. Unused vials should be refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F), protected from light, and stored in their carton until use. Reconstituted vials should be stored for up to 1 hour at room temperature, and any unused reconstituted solution should be discarded.
